moduleTitle: Lesson 8 - The Difference Between SOAP & REST
learningObjectives: State the core protocol and format differences between SOAP and REST.
Switch the System Under Test from the REST Coffeeshop to the SOAP DemoWebShop.
Scan the DemoWebShop's SOAP endpoint and rename Operations/Messages for clarity.
Send SOAP requests with account credentials and interpret the address/country responses.

studyGuide.sectionTitle: SOAP vs. REST, Recap and Reinforcement

rows: All conventional methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE...)
Usually HTTP, though REST can in principle use a different protocol (uncommon)
More flexible, though still less wide-spread than SOAP overall

elements.text: Both SOAP and REST are Web Services implementation methods riding on the same underlying protocol (HTTP) — they differ in how they leverage that protocol and which formats they support, not in the transport layer itself.

bulletPoints: SOAP = POST-only, XML-only. REST = any HTTP method, multiple formats.
REST's flexibility doesn't make it more common than SOAP in the wild — SOAP remains extremely widespread, especially in enterprise systems.

elements.description: The Coffeeshop used so far is a REST implementation. To explore SOAP, the course switches to the DemoWebShop — the same SUT used in AS1/AS2 — scanning its SOAP endpoint instead of a REST URI.

elements.title: Scanning the DemoWebShop SOAP endpoint
items: Create a new Component Folder as organizational best practice, then reopen the API Scan.

Rename Operations and Messages for clarity, since the API Scan sorts alphabetically: e.g. "AddToCart" → "02 Add To Cart", "CreateOrder" → "03 Create Order", "GetOrderCollection" → "04 Verify Order Placement".
Enter DemoWebShop account credentials (username/password) into the relevant request fields, e.g. "01 Get Address", and Run to retrieve the account's address.
Query the available countries via a "Get Country" style request to see the full countries list returned in the Response.

elements.text: Renaming Operations and Messages doesn't change their functionality at all — it's purely an organizational best practice, identical in spirit to the numbering convention already used for REST.

bulletPoints: SOAP and REST look and behave very similarly inside the API Scan itself — same Payload/Method/Params tabs, same Send/Run flow.
Getting the address and country list here sets up the values needed for later SOAP TestCases (billing/shipping address, order creation).

examPitfalls.title: Thinking REST can only use HTTP
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Candidates assume REST is strictly bound to HTTP, the same as SOAP.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: REST can, in principle, use a different transport protocol, though this is uncommon in practice. SOAP, by contrast, is always built on HTTP with POST as its only leverage method.

examPitfalls.title: Assuming renaming Operations changes their behavior
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Candidates worry that renaming a scanned SOAP Operation or Message will break its functionality.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Renaming Operations and Messages is purely organizational — it does not affect functionality at all. It exists purely so items sort logically despite the API Scan's alphabetical ordering.

examPitfalls.title: Forgetting SOAP requires credentials on every request
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Candidates send a SOAP request to the DemoWebShop without entering account username/password, expecting a valid response anyway.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Because SOAP is a stateless protocol, the server does not retain session data — the username/password (or equivalent credentials) must be sent with every single request that needs them.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which message format(s) does SOAP support?
practiceQuiz.hint: This is one of the two defining constraints of SOAP, alongside its HTTP method restriction.
practiceQuiz.rationale: SOAP only supports the XML message format. REST, by contrast, can work with a wider array of formats including XML, JSON, and plain text.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which SUT is scanned in this lesson to explore SOAP, and why?

options.text: The Coffeeshop, because it also supports SOAP.
The DemoWebShop, the same SUT used in AS1/AS2, because it is implemented using SOAP.
A brand-new banking demo application built for this lesson.
No SUT switch is needed — the Coffeeshop supports both implementation methods equally.

practiceQuiz.hint: The Coffeeshop used earlier in the course is a REST implementation — a different SUT is needed for SOAP.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The DemoWebShop, the exact same SUT used throughout AS1 and AS2, is implemented using SOAP, so the course switches to it to explore SOAP scanning and automation.

practiceQuiz.scenario: What effect does renaming a scanned SOAP Operation (e.g. "AddToCart" to "02 Add To Cart") have on its underlying functionality?

options.text: None — renaming is purely organizational and does not affect functionality.
It changes which HTTP Method the Operation uses.
It breaks the link to the underlying endpoint.
It converts the Operation from SOAP to REST.

practiceQuiz.hint: This is the same principle as the numerical-prefix convention used earlier for REST.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Renaming Operations and Messages doesn't affect their functionality at all — it's a best practice purely for organizing and clarifying the alphabetically-sorted list in the API Scan.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Why must a username and password be sent with every single SOAP request to the DemoWebShop in this lesson?

options.text: Because SOAP is a stateless protocol and the server doesn't retain your data between requests.
Because REST never requires credentials, unlike SOAP.
Because the DemoWebShop requires a Service Access Key instead of credentials.
This is only required for DELETE requests.

practiceQuiz.hint: Think about what "stateless" implies for repeated requests.
practiceQuiz.rationale: SOAP is a stateless protocol — the server doesn't retain data between calls — so every single request that needs authentication must include the username and password again.

quickRecap.value: POST only, XML only, built on HTTP.
All HTTP methods, multiple formats (XML/JSON/text), can (rarely) use a non-HTTP protocol.
Renaming Operations/Messages never changes their functionality — organization only.
Credentials must be sent with every request that needs them; nothing is remembered server-side.
